title: Amaral v. Cintas Corporation No. 2
lead: A uniform contractor promised Hayward to pay a living wage, then argued that the promise did not cover workers at its out-of-city plants.

actors.name: Production and stockroom employees
actors.role: Certified class seeking wages, benefits, and penalties

proceedings: Trial court: class certified; City intervened; summary rulings established coverage and liability; judgment and fee orders followed.
California Court of Appeal: affirmed judgment and appealed postjudgment orders, rejecting both sides’ challenges.
Rehearing and state Supreme Court review later denied.
limits: This is the 2008 California ordinance, contract, and penalty ruling. It does not certify current living-wage or Private Attorneys General Act law or decide the later Astra pharmaceutical-program dispute.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Hayward conditions its purchases on employee compensation
sections.cue: Introduce the ordinance and the work Cintas performed.
paragraphs: Hayward adopted a living wage ordinance in April 1999 for covered service contracts entered from July 1. Contracts exceeding $25,000 for listed services, including laundry, required initial hourly rates of $8 with health benefits or $9.25 without, subject to annual adjustments. The ordinance covered employees working on or under the authority of a City service contract, provided compensated time off, and required contractors to accept civil enforcement by aggrieved employees.

From July 1999 through June 2003, Cintas leased uniforms and janitorial items to Hayward, collected them weekly, and processed them in Union City and San Leandro. Production workers sorted, laundered, pressed, inspected, and reloaded items; stockroom workers replaced and repaired garments and handled labels and logos. City items were mixed with other customers’ items rather than assigned to separate workers. The City business generated less than one percent of the facilities’ revenue.

sections.title: Cintas repeatedly accepts compliance but pays below the required rates
sections.cue: Trace notice, certifications, and the resulting class action.
paragraphs: Before renewal, Hayward sent the complete ordinance and expressly made its purchase order subject to it. A Cintas manager signed a compliance certification in June 1999 without later recalling reading or discussing the ordinance. After notice of adjusted rates, another certification followed in 2000. Purchase orders also incorporated compliance. One fiscal year’s order was missing, but Cintas did not dispute the contract or the undertaking. It asked no clarifying questions during performance.

The employees sued June 23, 2003, asserting ordinance, Labor Code, unfair-competition, and contract violations. Another manager discovered the requirement in 2003, consulted a superior, and terminated the City contract by a July 3 letter. The court certified production and stockroom workers employed at both facilities from July 1, 1999 through June 30, 2003, and Hayward intervened. After the Private Attorneys General Act, or PAGA, became effective, the employees amended to seek additional penalties.

The trial court rejected an early extraterritoriality challenge. On September 23, 2005, it ruled on cross-motions for summary judgment or adjudication that the ordinance was constitutional, enforceable, applicable to all hours of covered employees, and violated by Cintas. Awards included $790,489 in wages, $14,254 in vacation benefits, and $258,900 in penalties. It found no willfulness justifying enhanced or waiting-time penalties. An appeal-facilitating stipulation produced judgment for the employees and City, later corrected in form. Both sides appealed the merits and postjudgment rulings.

sections.title: The City acts as purchaser rather than regulator of every outside employer
sections.cue: Explain the constitutional and coverage rulings.
paragraphs: Presiding Justice McGuiness, joined by Justices Pollak and Jenkins, distinguished Hayward’s proprietary contracting authority from general territorial regulation. The City could choose contractors and terms, with better compensation reasonably connected to service quality. Cintas could decline the business, as it eventually did. Employee enforcement and fines did not transform the condition into regulation of every outside employer.

The ordinance provided reasonable certainty despite unusual commingling arrangements. Its context and remedial purpose answered the vagueness challenge, and economic regulation allowed more flexibility than penal law. City officials’ testimony on statutory meaning was inadmissible legal opinion, even when given by a designated knowledgeable deposition representative. Cintas’s failure to inquire was not fatal by itself but weakened the claim of hopeless ambiguity.

Workers handling City uniforms acted under the service contract even though Cintas owned the garments and employed them. The claim that they served only their employer was waived and inconsistent with the text. A truncated attack on classification as laundry also failed, including because Cintas admitted supplying that service. Once a worker performed covered work, the ordinance required its rate for all that employee’s hours. Neither wages nor leave carried a City-minutes limitation, and there was no de minimis exception. Cintas could have segregated City work among a smaller group; the court did not cover employees with no City work at all.

sections.title: Commingling shifts the proof burden and the promise supplies beneficiary rights
sections.cue: Connect work allocation to contractual enforcement.
paragraphs: Employees established an inference that class members handled City items. Cintas controlled workflow, mixed the items, and admitted it lacked records identifying individual City assignments. Wage-law precedents and unequal access to proof justified requiring Cintas to identify workers who did no covered work. The absence of an express ordinance recordkeeping obligation did not defeat that burden shift.

The compliance promise was also sufficiently definite. Contract law favored enforcing ascertainable intentions; repeated undertakings and specified wages gave an ascertainable obligation. Civil Code § 1559 allowed nonparties to enforce contracts expressly made for their benefit where that intent appeared in the terms. As in prevailing-wage cases, an express wage promise to a public body plainly benefited the employees performing its work. They were intended beneficiaries entitled to sue for breach. Contract recovery remained a separate inquiry from any statutory private-action question.

sections.title: New enforcement standing does not retroactively create new penalties
sections.cue: Follow the statutory remedy issues separately.
paragraphs: PAGA allowed employees to pursue existing penalties previously collectible by the Labor Commissioner. That new standing did not change the legal consequences of past underpayments. Newly created liabilities were different: the vacation-pay penalty applied only to employees terminated after January 1, 2004, and plaintiffs did not seek newly increased rates for older violations. The amendments related back because they concerned the same underpayments and injuries, despite the newly available legal theory.

Cintas nevertheless avoided penalties requiring willfulness. A good-faith legal or factual defense could negate willfulness even if rejected. Its first-impression ordinance arguments were substantial rather than frivolous. Its conduct could be called cavalier, grossly negligent, or reckless, yet substantial evidence supported a good-faith belief that these workers were outside coverage. The court did not require the eventual litigation theory to have been formulated when payment came due. This did not make every unsuccessful defense automatically good faith.

Base liability remained. Cintas violated Labor Code § 223 by certifying required-scale payment to Hayward while secretly paying less; concealment could be from the contracting or enforcement party even if workers knew their actual wages. Section 227.3 required payment of vested vacation at termination. Employment agreements already provided vacation, and the ordinance added accrued entitlement. The $500 vacation penalty was limited to post-PAGA terminations.

sections.title: Good faith does not erase mandatory nonwillful penalties
sections.cue: Explain the rates and the court’s discretion.
paragraphs: Under the former versions of §§ 210 and 225.5, the $50 initial penalty applied per employee per pay period. Repetition did not automatically turn the second payday into a subsequent violation at twice the rate; notice that conduct violated the law marked that transition. Plaintiffs sought the former lower rates rather than later $100 and $200 rates, and the trial court properly used the initial rate.

Base penalties were mandatory, subject to PAGA’s power to reduce a maximum that would be unjust, arbitrary and oppressive, or confiscatory under its criteria. A dispute negating willfulness did not eliminate nonwillful violations. The court respected the Labor Commissioner’s persuasive interpretation about notice and pay periods, but rejected an informal policy excusing all penalties in good-faith disputes as contrary to statute. Its rulemaking defect likewise did not require forgiveness.

Considering notices, noncompliance, proportionality, and the financial evidence, the refusal to reduce $258,900 was within discretion. Cintas waived belated constitutional objections unsupported by argument. Most legal questions received de novo review; good-faith factual findings received substantial-evidence review, and penalty reduction and fee enhancement were discretionary questions.

sections.title: The affirmed judgment includes interest and fees but limits extra expenses
sections.cue: Close with both appeals and the precise monetary dispositions.
paragraphs: The judgment included contract interest of $372,546 plus $216.57 per day from April 29, 2006 to judgment. Cintas did not challenge that contract award, and the judgment prohibited double recovery. The appellate court therefore left unresolved whether identical interest could be awarded on unpaid-wage restitution under unfair-competition law; deciding it would provide no effective relief.

The trial court had awarded $1,199,550 in fees, using a $727,000 lodestar and 1.65 multiplier, plus $60,611 for the fee motion. Novel and difficult issues, skill, efficiency, and contingent nonpayment risk justified the multiplier. Risk did not require proof of particular paid work counsel had forgone, and the lodestar itself was uncontested.

Employees recovered $8,174.44 in statutory costs and another $498 for reasonable transcript and translation expenses. They could not recover $65,641.28 in other expenses, including experts, without statutory authority; Olson had disapproved the sole precedent they invoked. Their cross-appeal for greater penalties and expenses failed.

On June 11, 2008, the Court of Appeal affirmed the entire judgment and appealed postjudgment orders, awarding appellate costs to plaintiffs. No separate opinion appeared. Rehearing was denied July 2 and California Supreme Court review September 10; those later denials added no reasoned merits holding.
